title: 7 Reasons Men Struggle to Lose Weight | Phoenix
summary: Weight loss can stall for reasons beyond willpower. Learn 7 common barriers for men, from appetite and sleep to movement, muscle and medical factors. - Sep 26, 2026
body_markdown:
You start eating better. You get back to the gym. Maybe the scale moves for a few weeks, then suddenly it seems like nothing is happening.


It is easy to assume you need more discipline, fewer calories or a harder workout. But weight loss is affected by much more than willpower.


How much you eat, how filling those meals are, how much you move outside the gym, your sleep, muscle mass, health history and even medications can all affect progress.


These factors are not exclusive to men, but they can show up differently depending on body size, muscle mass, lifestyle and health. Understanding what may be getting in the way can help you make a better adjustment instead of simply trying harder.


## Quick takeaway


Weight loss is rarely controlled by one habit. Your food intake, appetite, daily movement, sleep, training, changing calorie needs and health history can all affect the result.


If progress has slowed, look at the whole picture before making your plan more restrictive.


## 1. You may be eating more than you think


Small extras such as drinks, sauces, snacks, restaurant meals and larger portions can reduce or erase the calorie deficit you expected to create.


Weight loss generally requires taking in less energy than your body uses over time. The difficult part is that the difference between maintenance and a calorie deficit can be smaller than it feels.


You do not need to be overeating dramatically for progress to slow. A few things that are easy to overlook can add up across the week, including alcohol, sweetened drinks, cooking oils, condiments, snacks while preparing food and larger weekend meals.


Your calorie needs can also change as your weight and activity change. A target that created a deficit several months ago may not create the same deficit today.


That does not mean you need to count every calorie forever. Instead, use tracking as a temporary reality check when your expectations and results stop matching.


**Worth checking:** Before cutting food further, check whether your current calorie target still matches your current weight and activity.[Calculate your estimated daily calorie needs.](https://www.phoenix.ca/tools/tdee-calculator)


## 2. Your meals may not be keeping you full


A diet can fit your calorie target and still be difficult to maintain if your meals regularly leave you hungry.


Weight loss is much harder to maintain when you spend most of the day thinking about your next meal.


Instead of looking only at calories, look at what those calories contain.


Meals built around protein foods, vegetables, fruit, whole grains and other fibre-rich foods can give your diet more structure and nutritional value. Canada’s Food Guide recommends regularly eating vegetables and fruit, whole grains and protein foods, with plant-based protein foods chosen more often.


There is no single ideal diet for everyone. Obesity Canada recommends a personalized approach that considers preferences, culture, affordability and what someone can realistically maintain over the long term.


The goal is not to find the most restrictive meal plan. It is to find one that helps you consistently eat in a way that supports your goals without feeling like every day is a fight against hunger.


**Worth remembering:** The best eating pattern is not necessarily the strictest one. It is one you can realistically maintain.


## 3. Your workout may be only a small part of your day


Going to the gym helps, but your total daily movement also includes walking, standing, commuting, chores and everything else you do outside a workout.


A hard workout can feel like a lot of activity, but it still represents only a small part of a 24-hour day.


Your total daily energy use includes your resting needs, planned exercise, digestion and everyday movement such as walking around the office, taking the stairs, doing housework or running errands.


That means two men who complete the same workout can still have very different daily energy expenditure depending on how active they are during the rest of the day.


Regular physical activity has benefits even when the scale does not change dramatically. Obesity Canada notes that aerobic activity can support modest weight and fat loss, reduce abdominal visceral fat, improve fitness and help with weight maintenance.


Instead of judging your plan only by gym sessions, look at your entire week of movement.


**Worth remembering:** A workout matters, but so does what happens during the other 23 hours of your day.[See how daily movement affects your TDEE.](https://www.phoenix.ca/tools/tdee-calculator)


## 4. You may not be getting enough sleep


Poor sleep can make weight management harder by increasing hunger, affecting food choices and making it more difficult to stay consistent with healthy habits.


Food and exercise usually get most of the attention in weight loss plans. Sleep deserves a place in the conversation too.


Controlled studies have found that restricting sleep can increase subjective hunger and daily energy intake. In one meta-analysis of randomized trials, people consumed more calories during periods of sleep restriction compared with normal sleep.


There is also a practical side to this.


When you are exhausted, cooking, exercising and sticking to a routine can become harder. Convenience food becomes more appealing, workouts are easier to skip and late-night eating may become more common.


Sleep alone is not a weight loss strategy, and getting an extra hour does not guarantee the number on the scale will change.


But if you are carefully managing food and activity while regularly sleeping poorly, sleep may be one part of your plan worth addressing.


**Worth remembering:** Nutrition and exercise are easier to manage when you are not constantly running on empty.


## 5. You may be ignoring muscle while chasing the scale


Resistance training may help maintain muscle or fat-free mass during weight management, which matters even if it does not create dramatic changes on the scale by itself.


When the goal is weight loss, it is tempting to measure success using only one number.


But losing weight and improving body composition are not exactly the same thing.


Resistance training gives your muscles a reason to keep adapting while your overall body weight changes. Obesity Canada notes that resistance training may help maintain or modestly increase muscle mass or fat-free mass and improve mobility in adults living with overweight or obesity.


This can be especially relevant for men who already carry more muscle and want to maintain strength while losing weight.


Cardio and resistance training do not need to compete with each other. They serve different purposes.


Instead of trying to burn as many calories as possible every time you exercise, consider whether your weekly routine also includes some form of progressive resistance training.


**Worth remembering:** Do not judge every workout by how many calories it burns. Strength and muscle retention matter too.[Read what men should know about muscle during weight loss.](https://www.phoenix.ca/blog/glp1-men-canada)


## 6. Your plan may not have changed as your body changed


The calorie needs you had at the beginning of weight loss may not be the same after your weight, activity or routine changes.


A plan can work well and then stop producing the same result.


That does not necessarily mean your body has somehow become impossible to change.


As your weight changes, the amount of energy your body uses can also change. Your activity may have changed too. You may be walking less, training differently or eating slightly larger portions without noticing.


This is why a plateau is often a useful time to reassess rather than immediately make a drastic cut.


Look at your weight trend over several weeks instead of reacting to a few days. Then review your current estimated calorie needs, portions, activity and consistency.


Phoenix already has a deeper guide covering some of the common calorie-deficit mistakes that can cause progress to stall.


The important point is simple: the plan that got you here may need an adjustment to get you to the next stage.


**Worth remembering:** A plateau is information. Use it to reassess the plan before making it more extreme.[See 5 calorie deficit mistakes that can stall weight loss.](https://www.phoenix.ca/blog/calorie-deficit-mistakes-weight-loss)


## 7. There may be more going on than diet and exercise


Sleep problems, health conditions, pain, medications and other individual factors can make weight management more complicated for some people.


Sometimes the answer is not another diet adjustment.


Obesity Canada notes that disrupted sleep, pain, metabolic conditions, some psychiatric conditions and certain medications can contribute to challenges with weight management.


That is one reason obesity care is increasingly approached as more than a simple equation of eating less and moving more.


For some adults, behavioural changes may be enough. Others may benefit from additional support, including medical nutrition therapy, behavioural care, prescription weight management treatment or other approaches depending on their health and eligibility.


Canada’s current obesity guidelines describe pharmacotherapy as one of the evidence-based options that can be considered for appropriate adults alongside health behaviour changes.


A licensed healthcare provider can review your health history, medications, goals and other factors to help identify whether something else may be affecting your progress.


**Worth remembering:** If you have made consistent changes and progress remains difficult, it may be worth looking beyond calories alone.[Learn about weight loss treatment in Canada.](https://www.phoenix.ca/treatments/weight-loss)


## Weight loss is more than willpower


When weight loss is not going the way you expected, the answer is not always to eat less or exercise harder.


Start by looking at the complete picture.


Are your current calorie needs different from when you started? Are your meals filling enough? How much are you moving outside the gym? Are you sleeping well? Are you doing anything to maintain muscle? Has your plan changed as your body changed?


And if those pieces seem solid, consider whether a health or medication-related factor is worth discussing with a licensed healthcare provider.


Sustainable weight management usually comes from making the right adjustment, not automatically making the plan more extreme.
